claims.statement: Custom source, transform, and sink logic lives in HTTP services referenced by pipe components; URL systems connect to existing services while microservice systems also provision the adapter, without changing the role's protocol.
A custom JSON source retrieves entity arrays with JSON Pull GETs, while a custom JSON push sink POSTs JSON Push batches to a URL or microservice endpoint.

The HTTP endpoint source registers /api/receivers/{pipe_id}/entities and writes incoming entities to its pipe's sink; no pump is configured and POSTs are the only way entities flow through that source.
The HTTP endpoint sink registers /api/publishers/{pipe_id}/entities and has no pump; entities flow through it when clients retrieve them, using the protocol compatible with a JSON source.
Publisher URL query parameters are bound to the DTL variable _B, allowing publisher transforms to use request-specific values.
Dataset entity reads at /api/datasets/{dataset_id}/entities support JSON Pull, including indexed subset retrieval.
URL systems represent remote HTTP/HTTPS servers and supply session handling, connection pooling, and authentication; a custom source service may run anywhere reachable over HTTP from Sesam.
URL system url_pattern substitutes relative URLs at %s, or appends them when %s is absent; base_url is deprecated and exactly one of base_url and url_pattern must be configured.

REST systems extend URL systems with named HTTP operations and mapping configuration; REST components are recommended for non-Sesam APIs, and REST sources support body or link-header pagination and continuation in query parameters or headers.
REST operations may be defined on the system or source, sink, or transform, with component definitions taking precedence; secret-bearing operation definitions must be on the system.
JSON Pull and JSON Push specify array bodies even for one entity; the Sesam HTTP receiver additionally accepts a single JSON object and requires Content-Type application/json.
Entities are string-keyed dictionaries with literal, list, or dictionary values, and require a string _id unique to a logical entity within a flow, while multiple versions may share that identity.
A source entity may omit _deleted, defaulting to not deleted; Boolean true marks it deleted, and the entity model interprets other values as not deleted.
An entity's _updated marker must be a string or integer, is opaque to parties other than the producing source, and can be passed back as the since query parameter for continuation.

Root-level underscore-prefixed fields are reserved and, except for _id and _deleted, are ignored as stored input when writing to a dataset; nested child dictionaries are exempt, and source _updated is still usable for continuation.

Exported dataset entities contain generated metadata such as _updated, _hash, _previous, and _ts; JSON push sinks include reserved fields, so target adapters may need to remove metadata while interpreting _deleted as a deletion.

Sesam's JSON extension types use Transit-style strings: ~: for namespaced identifiers, ~r for URI, ~t for Date and Datetime, ~b for base64 Bytes, ~u for hexadecimal UUID, and ~f for arbitrary-precision Decimal.
Unrecognized Transit tags are treated as strings, and the entity-model documentation states there is no escape support for literal strings beginning with ~.
Transit Datetime values require date and time in UTC with a final Z and support optional fractions with up to nanosecond precision.

Decimal values have arbitrary precision while Float values use IEEE 754 binary64 and may lose precision; HTTP receivers default do_float_as_decimal and do_float_as_int to true, converting fractional numbers to Decimal and zero-fraction numbers to Integer.

JSON Pull since requests entities after the _updated token supplied, omitting since requests the beginning, and ordered-stream continuation can use the last returned entity's marker; the documented since=21 example begins at offset 22.
JSON Pull limit is an integer entity-count cap for splitting streams across requests, with no protocol limit by default although endpoints may choose another default.

JSON Pull subset is a JSON-encoded optional expression: a supported but missing subset returns 404, whereas an endpoint without subset support may ignore it; documented indexed subsets use an eq expression and query values must be URL-encoded.
The JSON source defaults supports_since to false, is_since_comparable to true, and is_chronological to false; enabling supports_since adds the since parameter to requests.

Continuation tracking prioritizes a chronological strategy when supports_since and is_chronological are true, otherwise uses the maximum marker when supports_since and is_since_comparable are true, and otherwise disables tracking; chronology permits checkpointing within interrupted runs whereas unordered sources require rereading the failed request.

Continuation state is stored in the pump's pipe_offset and can be read or manually updated/reset through the Service API; initial import or reset normally starts without since, but initial_since_value can override that starting point.

JSON source page_size must be at least 1, is sent as limit, and makes the source request pages until no more data remains; paging requires supports_since, is_chronological, and is_since_comparable all true.

The continuation tutorials demonstrate mapping a remote modification field into _updated and translating incoming since into an API-specific changed-record request; the unordered example uses max tracking and cannot claim chronological support.
JSON Pull X-Dataset-Populated conveys true or false, and an absent header means the populated state is unknown rather than false.

X-Dataset-Max-Updated is the JSON-encoded highest committed offset and should appear in the last entity of a complete retrieval, except a stream marked X-Dataset-Filtered true need not include that entity, such as a publisher with a transform.

JSON Pull X-Dataset-Generation identifies dataset creation and changes on delete/recreate, while X-Dataset-Restore-Uuid identifies a restore and X-Dataset-Restore-Offset gives the JSON-encoded highest committed offset at that restore.
JSON Pull X-Dataset-Completeness, when present, is an integer number of microseconds since the Unix epoch representing dataset completeness.
Automatic reprocessing uses JSON Pull dataset-state headers to know when to rewind or reset, but the default reprocessing_policy is continue rather than automatic reset.
Continuation imports cannot infer deletion from absence in a delta response; deletion entities or periodic full rescans are needed to account for records disappearing from the source.
For JSON snapshot imports, if_source_empty defaults to accept, allowing previously synchronized entities to be deleted by an empty source; fail instead fails the import and preserves prior entities.
A source adapter must expose upstream errors as failures rather than successful entity arrays, because Sesam may otherwise treat the import as successfully complete.

An HTTP transform is a POST request-response operation that must accept and return application/json arrays, can return zero or more transformed, filtered, or newly created entities, and raises an exception on non-2xx responses rather than acting as a JSON Push synchronization session.
HTTP transform output is passed to later transformation stages and the sink; documented configurations use a later DTL stage to copy the returned data and supply _id.
HTTP transforms require system and url, support string-valued request headers, and split requests according to batch_size, whose default is 100.

HTTP transform side_effects defaults to true to protect against unintended external changes through features such as pipe preview; false is appropriate only when effects are absent or explicitly acceptable.
HTTP transform trigger_on selects entities by a property and value with substring wildcards and default key _trigger; missing or nonmatching values pass through without transformation.

JSON Push uses a string sequence_id per sync, a string request_id per request, and previous_request_id referencing the preceding request except on the first; sequence IDs are recommended to be UUIDs and request IDs are local to the sequence.
JSON Push is_full is a Boolean included in requests and defaults false; is_first and is_last are true only on the first and last requests respectively of a full synchronization.

Incremental JSON Push accepts supplied entities and may ignore synchronization parameters, with omitted parameters treated as incremental; it does not infer deletions from records no longer included in pushes.
Only one full JSON Push sequence should be active at a time; a different full sequence_id replaces the active one, is_last ends its scope, and incremental requests do not affect the active sequence.
A completed full JSON Push sync marks previously existing entities absent from the supplied complete sequence as deleted.
The documented JSON Push full-sync examples expose dataset updates between batch requests, so the contract examples do not represent an all-batches atomic commit.

The Sesam JSON push sink defaults batch_size to 100 and always sends a final empty batch, so sending 150 entities produces batches of 100, 50, and 0; protocol clients may alternatively include entities in their is_last request.
During full JSON Push, the server should return 409 for a predecessor request_id mismatch, a changed is_full within the sequence, or is_first true when it knows the request is not first.
A JSON push sink receiving 409 must stop the active sync and try later; a full sync must restart from the beginning with a new sequence rather than just retrying the disputed batch.
A custom sink's responsibility includes making a legacy target appear idempotent and handling deletion metadata, because repeated non-idempotent target writes can produce different results.

Microservice systems require docker.image and docker.port, determine their own base address, and support private image repositories using docker.username and docker.password, separately from HTTP service credentials.

The documented single-machine architecture provisions user microservices as individual Docker containers, while the clustered architecture provisions them as individual Kubernetes deployments; the self-hosted Kubernetes installation guide is marked draft.

Managed microservices use HTTP by default and use_https enables HTTPS; URL and microservice certificate verification defaults false, and URL custom_ca_pem_chain supplies verification certificates when verify_ssl is true.

Microservice IDs are local-network domain names constrained to 2–63 characters, an ASCII letter or number initially, and letters, numbers, underscores or hyphens thereafter; lower-case letters are advised to avoid DNS lookup errors.

Microservice docker.hosts provides container-local hostname/IP mappings, URL systems support HTTP(S)/SOCKS5 proxies, and the Service API proxy forwards requests to managed routes at /api/systems/{system_id}/proxy/{rest_of_path}.

docker.skip_pull defaults false and microservice restarts, including configuration changes, attempt to pull an image; docker.pull_image_cron_expression schedules image pulls and restarts the container if a newer version is pulled.

Microservice eager_load false permits delaying startup when no pipes reference the service, while true forces startup and overrides service metadata; its documented default is true except false on developer subscriptions.

Microservice docker.memory defaults to 128 MB, and the documentation warns that container resource use affects the node and recommends small containers and streaming rather than storing complete transfers in adapter memory.

Configuration values can reference $ENV and $SECRET, and docker.environment passes strings unchanged but serializes non-string values as JSON strings; adapter-wide values, endpoint-specific URL values, and protocol state parameters serve distinct configuration scopes.
Secrets are write-only and intended for credentials, with local secrets recommended; deleting and re-adding a system removes its system-local secrets, requiring re-upload.
Most Service API calls use a JWT supplied as Authorization: Bearer followed by the token, and actions are controlled by permissions; Pull and Push examples use the equivalent lowercase bearer scheme.

URL authentication is opt-in with basic, digest, ntlm, tripletex, or jwt, requires scheme-appropriate credentials, and JWT authentication requires jwt_token and overwrites Authorization set through system headers.

Microservice HTTP authentication is opt-in with basic or digest, and username/password have no effect without selecting authentication; adapter upstream authentication remains custom implementation logic supplied with its own credentials.

URL OAuth2 supports client-credentials and refresh-token grants, cannot be combined with JWT authentication or jwt_token, requires TLS token and target endpoints, and defaults refresh_window to 30 seconds before expiry.

Receiver validation_expression renders a Jinja template on each request, accepts empty output and reports nonempty output as an error, and exposes url, request_params, request_headers, secret access, and filters such as decode_jwt.

Receiver custom validation without JWT assumes write_data permission granted to group:Anonymous; system secrets take precedence over same-named global secrets, and using them requires the pipe to have permission to read the system.
Receiver POSTs set sink-dataset completeness to current time by default, but a positive integer X-Dataset-Completeness header overrides it, with microseconds since epoch recommended.
HTTP endpoint source auto_populate_dataset defaults true, initially marking the sink dataset populated, and can only be specified for dataset sinks.
URL and microservice systems default connect_timeout to 60 seconds and read_timeout to 1800 seconds for their HTTP connections to the service.

URL retry_strategy, also referenced by microservice systems, sets status-code-dependent pump defaults using codes, ranges, lists, or default, with directly configured pump values taking priority; it supports max_read_retries, read_retry_delay, write_retry_delay, max_retries_per_entity, max_consecutive_write_errors, max_write_errors_in_retry_dataset, and batch_retries.

The documented retry_strategy example disables retries for 400-428 writes, delays 429 retries by 30 seconds, and delays selected 500/502/504 retries by 60 seconds; these are example policies rather than defaults.

Pumps own entity processing, failed-write retries, execution logging, and optional dead letters; defaults include zero read retries, termination at the first consecutive write error, and zero accepted retry-dataset write errors, which effectively disables failed-write retries there.
For batched writes, pump batch_retries defaults to 3 and fallback_to_single_entities_on_batch_fail defaults true, allowing single-entity fallback when a batch fails.

Managed adapter logs can be inspected in the system Status page, while system APIs expose logs, status, reload, and proxy; pipe execution logs provide failures and continuation diagnostics such as pipe_offset and processed_last_run.

Receiver trace defaults off and can log request/response headers and body prefixes in execution events; body prefix defaults are 100 bytes, Authorization redaction defaults to 600 bytes, and log_secret_redacted_bytes -1 redacts the whole Authorization header.

This documentation hands custom-adapter implementation off to external starter repositories, including Python source, transform, and sink templates and ASP.NET, Java, and NodeJS source templates, rather than providing validated current implementations in this repository.

The documented Sesam client test workflow uses expected/<pipe>.json and expected/<pipe>.test.json fixtures and sesam -vv test to verify endpoint-pipe output, recommending that output pipes be disabled or unable to write to real target systems during tests.
